extracted.intended_audience: economists, labour‑market researchers, public policy makers, and students interested in Quebec employment dynamics
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical/report study of Quebec's employment and unemployment (1946–1989/1990), presenting definitions, metrics, comparative tables, and five hypothesized structural causes for persistently high unemployment. Uses Statistics Canada survey definitions and historical time‑series comparisons to diagnose regional and demographic patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: activity, employment, unemployment (StatsCan monthly survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses Statistics Canada monthly labour force survey definitions for population aged 15+, classifying people as inactive (not looking for work), active (in labour force), employed (holding a job), and unemployed (not employed but looking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tableau 1 shows the definition tree and Québec figures for 1989. These canonical definitions underlie all rate calculations and comparisons; the text notes the choice of 1989 (or 1988) to avoid 1990–91 recession distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity rate (taux d'activité)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activity rate = Actifs / Population (15+); measures the share of the adult population participating in the labour force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Québec 1989 activity rate = 3,343 / 5,222 = 64.0%. The report stresses that a lower activity rate reflects under‑utilization of human resources and contributes substantially to Québec's employment deficit relative to Ontario.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unemployment rate (taux de chômage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unemployment rate = Chômeurs / Actifs; proportion of labour‑force participants who are unemployed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Québec 1989 unemployment rate = 311 / 3,343 = 9.3%. The text warns this measure can be ambiguous because monthly flows between inactivity and activity are large and some jobseekers are not 'very active' in searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment–population ratio (rapport emploi‑population)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employment–population ratio = Employés / Population (15+); used increasingly as a measure of the economy's overall capacity to put its population to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Québec 1989 = 3,031 / 5,222 = 58.0%. The authors argue this ratio complements the unemployment rate by reflecting participation and employment simultaneously; it is used to compare Québec with Ontario and other regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic perspective: flows (entry and exit rates) matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Unemployment should be interpreted dynamically: the stock of unemployed depends on the monthly rates of entry into unemployment and exit from unemployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report emphasizes that roughly 40% of those unemployed in one month are no longer unemployed the next (half find a job, half become inactive). Thus two distinct dimensions affect unemployment: instability (high entry) and difficulty of finding work (slow exit). Comparative differences (Europe vs North America) are framed in terms of stable/rare vs unstable/abundant employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative severity indicators: involuntary separations, duration, search intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess unemployment seriousness by (1) share of involuntary job loss among the unemployed, (2) average duration of unemployment, and (3) intensity of job search (e.g., direct contact with employers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 1989 Québec: 68.2% of Québec unemployed had experienced involuntary job loss vs 54.9% in Ontario; average duration 5 months in Québec vs 3 in Ontario; >75% of Québec jobseekers used direct contact with employers. These indicators show Québec unemployment is both more often involuntary and longer lasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part‑time and involuntary part‑time employment as indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure share of part‑time work (<30 hours/week) and share of involuntary part‑time (workers wanting full‑time but only finding part‑time) to capture shortages of full‑time employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1989 figures: part‑time employment was 13.5% in Québec vs 15.5% in Ontario, but involuntary part‑time was twice as frequent in Québec (4.3% of all jobs vs 2.1% in Ontario), indicating scarcity of full‑time jobs forcing workers into unwanted part‑time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry/sectoral employment structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine distribution of employment across broad industrial sectors (primary, manufacturing, tertiary) and detailed manufacturing specializations to understand structural differences between regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tableau 7 and 8 compare Québec and Ontario: both have ~20% manufacturing, but Ontario is more concentrated in durable goods (automotive, metals, electrical) while Québec retains higher shares in textiles, clothing, wood and paper. Sectoral specialization differences can explain differential employment outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education level as employment determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Use employment and unemployment rates by education level to assess how schooling affects labour market attachment and vulnerability to cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1989 example: very low employment and high unemployment for those not beyond grade 8 (only ~31% employed), while university graduates had ~81% employment and only ~4.7% unemployment. Less‑educated groups are far more sensitive to cyclical downturns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and sex demographic breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Report activity, employment and unemployment rates by age and sex groups to reveal demographic patterns such as youth unemployment and female labour force participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: women are less active than men (62% vs 83% for 15–64 in Québec), youth (15–24) unemployment is much higher (13.1% vs 8.5% for 25–64), and regional and temporal trends (e.g., rising female participation since 1949) are important for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative regional and urban analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare Québec with other provinces (Ontario, Prairies, Atlantic provinces), specific US regions/states, and metropolitan areas to contextualize performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables compare Québec 1988–89 rates to Ontario and US regions; Montréal had the highest unemployment among Canadian metro areas >200k in 1989, and Québec showed substantial deficit (~430,000 jobs) compared with Ontario in 1989.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical time‑series comparability adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust historical unemployment and employment‑population series to be comparable over time (corrections for methodological changes in series construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote explains that official rates in 1948, 1956, 1966, 1974 were revised upward slightly to be comparable with post‑1975 StatsCan methodology; similar raccordement applied to employment–population series used in figures 1–3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five hypothesized structural causes for rising structural unemployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame structural drift in unemployment as potentially arising from five phenomena: (1) demographic congestion from baby‑boom and female labour entry; (2) easier access to unemployment insurance (UI) benefits; (3) wage pushes from construction/public sector/minimum wage and their locomotive effects; (4) deep structural mutations in Quebec's economy; (5) persistence caused by anti‑inflation policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second part of the study focuses analytically on these five causes (listed in order) to explain the paradox of rising productivity alongside high unemployment; each cause is then examined in subsequent sections (e.g., 2.2 discusses demographic congestion, UI reform effects are discussed in the following paragraphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of search method indicators to evaluate search intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate job search seriousness using indicators such as direct contact with employers versus other search methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that >75% of Québec jobseekers used direct contact with employers in 1989 (vs ~65% in other regions), making this a common metric for assessing search intensity and comparing search behaviour across provinces.
